summary: LISP aims to improve routing scalability through address role separation, encapsulation and mapping. Drawing on implementation work, deployment experience and theoretical studies, this informational RFC discusses the effects LISP deployment can have on the routing infrastructure and on end users.

eli5.summary: Like separating a person's name from their current street address. This looks at what that trick means for the Internet's routers and for users.

questions: how does lisp improve routing scalability
what is the difference between eids and rlocs
what are the operational challenges of lisp
how does lisp support ipv6 transition
subtitle: How separating network addresses from network locations changes routing.

tldr.problem: Internet routing is not scaling well: routing tables grow too large and change too frequently, making it hard for routers to forward packets efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: LISP separates addresses into two types: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) that identify a device, and Routing Locators (RLOCs) that show where on the network it is. A mapping system translates between them, allowing smaller routing tables and fine-grained traffic control.
tldr.outcome: Experience from implementations, deployments, and research shows LISP can scale routing and enables traffic engineering, IPv6 transition, and multicast, but introduces new operational challenges in resiliency, troubleshooting, and business models.

facts.label: RIB reduction
facts.value: Up to one order of magnitude

today: RFC 7834 documents the impact of LISP deployment based on implementation and research experience. LISP has been deployed in production networks, particularly by content delivery operators and service providers, and the document's findings remain relevant for understanding the trade-offs of locator/ID separation approaches.

sections.title: Why LISP Matters
sections.content:
The Internet's routing system, which directs packets from one place to another, has a scaling problem. Every network that wants to be reachable from anywhere needs to announce its address block to the global routing system. The system keeps growing, routing tables get larger, and stability suffers.

LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) attacks this problem by separating the concept of a network address into two different roles. An Endpoint Identifier (EID) is like your name—it identifies who you are. A Routing Locator (RLOC) is like your street address—it tells routers where you are in the network topology. By separating these, LISP lets the routing system handle only locators (which are aggregatable like phone-company regional centers), while keeping identifiers out of the global routing system.
sections.eli5: Your mailing address and your name are different things. Right now, the Internet conflates them: every organization has to publish its address block everywhere. LISP separates them, so routers only need to know about aggregatable location addresses, not every individual network's identity.

sections.title: How LISP Works
sections.content:
LISP uses three core principles: address role separation, encapsulation, and mapping. When a host sends a packet to a remote destination, the packet arrives at an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) at its network boundary. The ITR looks up the destination EID in a mapping system to find which Egress Tunnel Routers (ETRs) can reach that destination. The packet is then encapsulated: wrapped in a new IP header with the ITR as source and an ETR as destination, then forwarded through the Internet to that ETR. The ETR unwraps the packet and delivers it to the actual destination.

The mapping system is the key difference from traditional routing. Instead of every EID being advertised globally (a push model), LISP uses a pull model: routers request mappings on demand when they encounter unknown destinations. The mapping associates each EID prefix with a list of RLOCs, annotated with priority and weight values for traffic engineering.
sections.eli5: You write a letter (EID source to EID destination) and put it in an envelope (RLOC source to RLOC destination) to get it from your local post office to the recipient's. The post office looks up a directory to find which regional hub serves the destination, then sends the envelope there.

sections.title: What LISP Enables
sections.content:
Routing Scalability: Research studies show LISP can reduce the Routing Information Base (RIB)—the size of routing tables—by an order of magnitude. Because only aggregatable locators are in the global routing system, not individual EID prefixes, routing is independent of the overall Internet size and depends mainly on traffic patterns.

Traffic Engineering: LISP gives sites fine-grained control over incoming and outgoing traffic. A site can assign different RLOCs different priorities and weights for each EID prefix, directing traffic to specific paths. Notably, each Map-Request includes the source EID, allowing a site to give different answers depending on which network is asking—something BGP cannot do.

IPv6 Transition: LISP's encapsulation works with any combination of address families. A data center can run IPv4 internally but offer IPv6 to the outside world by deploying xTRs (Ingress/Egress Tunnel Routers) that tunnel IPv6 over IPv4.

Multicast: LISP supports inter-domain multicast, and related work like LISP Replication Engineering (LISP-RE) can construct multicast distribution trees even when the core network lacks multicast support.
sections.eli5: LISP shrinks routing tables, lets networks choose which path traffic takes (like picking preferred shipping routes for different types of cargo), helps move from IPv4 to IPv6 without wholesale rewiring, and supports group messaging across domains.

sections.title: Operational Challenges
sections.content:
Resiliency and Troubleshooting: LISP's flexibility comes at a cost. When an ITR fails, traffic is rerouted to other ITRs, but those may not yet have the mappings needed—causing a burst of mapping requests and potential packet loss. Failure recovery using existing monitoring is slow (seconds, not milliseconds). Troubleshooting is harder because operators only see their local cache and partial view of the mapping system. ICMP error messages carry only the first few bytes of the original packet, which may not be enough for diagnosis.

MTU and Encapsulation: Encapsulation adds an extra IP header, reducing the available space for payload and potentially causing fragmentation. In practice, modern systems handle this well.

Middleboxes and Filtering: Firewalls and intrusion detection systems that expect to see the original packet header are confused by LISP encapsulation. If the encapsulated traffic is also encrypted, middleboxes cannot inspect it and may drop legitimate packets. LISP-aware firewalls that inspect the inner packet are needed.

Transition to Non-LISP Sites: To reach networks that do not support LISP, proxy tunnel routers (PxTRs) are needed. These introduce path stretch (longer routes than necessary) and raise questions about where to deploy them, how many are needed, and who operates them.

Business and Operational Models: Unclear answers remain about how EIDs will be allocated, who will operate the mapping infrastructure, and how different mapping systems interoperate.
sections.eli5: When a router dies, recovery is slow and packets get lost. The extra wrapping reduces message space. Firewalls do not understand encapsulated traffic. Connecting to non-LISP networks adds extra hops. Nobody is sure who should run the mapping service or how to allocate addresses fairly.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC notes that security analysis is detailed in RFC 7835. LISP's security depends critically on the control plane—the mapping system. Attacks on the mapping system must be prevented through authentication and authorization. LISP specifications include mechanisms for securing control-plane messages and authenticating mappings. Like other IP-in-IP technologies, LISP's data plane (the encapsulation itself) is secure when gleaning (learning mappings from data-plane packets) is disabled.

This document is informational and published in April 2016. It synthesizes years of implementation work, real-world deployment experience, and research. The open questions it raises remain important for future LISP development, but the protocol has proven feasible and valuable for specific use cases, especially for operators and content delivery networks.
sections.eli5: LISP must protect the mapping directory from tampering. The encapsulation itself is not the weak point—the real question is whether the mapping service is trustworthy.
